title: Responding to Microaggressions With Care and Purpose
before: Explore how DSD staff respond to subtle exclusion in ways that restore participation and preserve the affected person’s choices.

turns.text: This course is Responding to Microaggressions With Care and Purpose. It’s about moments when a remark or action sends a message of devaluation or exclusion related to identity, including race, and someone has to decide what to do next. The course starts with a practical question: what does a response in this moment actually need to accomplish?

It offers several purposes. A response might restore a question, correct an assumption, return credit, or offer support. It also asks us to describe the specific words or action, because the possible message and the speaker’s intention are different questions. That framing takes some pressure off. You’re responding to an action, not judging a whole person.

The opening case is in a service setting. A person asks a question about service information, and a staff member says they’re “surprisingly articulate.” The question never gets answered. You’ll practice choosing a response. Before you choose, notice what happened to the person’s question, and what the remark assumed about competence.

Which connects to intention. A well-meant remark can still displace a contribution or carry an unsupported assumption. The course suggests addressing the particular action and what needs to change, without turning the response into a debate about whether the speaker is a good person. Identity assumptions can quietly shape whose expertise seems expected and whose account seems credible.

The course names three ways to respond in the moment. Clarification asks what supports an assumption. A brief boundary names a needed change. Redirection restores the contribution or the task. No sentence works everywhere, so you choose based on purpose, setting, and your role. And uncertainty about perfect wording doesn’t mean doing nothing.

Role and safety matter, too. A response could increase unwanted attention for the person affected, so sometimes appropriate help or a later response fits better. In one practice situation, a colleague’s policy proposal is interrupted and later repeated as someone else’s idea, and you heard the original. You’ll consider which response best restores it.

Support has its own boundaries. The course suggests offering a specific choice, like “Would a follow-up from me be useful?” or “Would you prefer some space?” The person may want another response, or none. An offer of support doesn’t authorize sharing their account, recording it, or deciding what outcome they should want.

There’s also a formal side. A supportive conversation is different from an established reporting or review process, and you follow the responsibilities that apply to your role. You don’t need agreement on the term microaggression, an apology, or consultant guidance before acting on an actual duty. If you describe what happened, describe it accurately, without inferred motives.

The third practice situation involves a community contributor who’s asked to interpret because staff inferred a language from their appearance. Nobody checked their skills, interest, or role. You’ll weigh how to correct the assumption. As you do, consider what the correction itself might ask of the contributor in front of the group.

The course also looks at patterns. Repeated interruption, lost credit, or identity-based assignments can shape whose work is visible, which affects development and retention. A corrected meeting note can show that credit was restored, but it doesn’t prove exclusion ended. Near the end, you’ll privately write a short reply to a practice exchange and consider what it could change and what burden it might add.

As you go through the course, think of a moment from your own work when something didn’t sit right and you weren’t sure what to say. What would a response have needed to accomplish? Bring that moment with you, privately. The course won’t hand you a script, but it can help you choose with more purpose next time.

guidance.title: Choosing among three responses
guidance.text: Clarifying, setting a boundary, and redirecting each do different work. A clarifying question about what an assumption is based on can open reflection, though it may also invite debate. A brief boundary is direct and short. Redirection returns attention to the person’s question or idea. Before choosing, ask what the moment most needs and what your role allows you to do well.

guidance.title: What your response could change
guidance.text: Look at the reply you wrote. What did it set out to do: clarify, set a boundary, or restore a contribution? Consider who would carry the effort if your response led to a longer exchange. Is there a version that accomplishes the same purpose with less burden on the person affected, and what would still remain unresolved afterward?
